title: Breakfast at a café in Madrid
setting: It's 9 a.m. in a busy neighbourhood café near Retiro Park in Madrid. Locals are standing at the bar with a coffee and a slice of toast before work. The waiter looks up from the coffee machine.
objectives: Order a coffee the way people do in Spanish bars
Order a typical Spanish breakfast toast
Understand "for here or to take away?"
Ask to pay and know what to do about tipping
varietyNote: These phrases are typical of everyday Spanish in Madrid and much of Spain. Bar Spanish varies by region — in Catalonia you'll hear "pa amb tomàquet" (Catalan) for tomato bread, for example — and Latin American Spanish often orders differently (see the Mexico City adventure).

phrases.text: ¿Me pones un café con leche, por favor?
phrases.translation: Can I get a coffee with milk, please?
phrases.example: Hola, ¿me pones un café con leche y una tostada?
phrases.exampleTranslation: Hi, can I get a coffee with milk and a slice of toast?
phrases.note: "Ponerme" (literally "put me") is the everyday way to order in a Spanish bar. It sounds direct to English speakers, but it's normal and friendly.

alsoHeard.text: Quería un café con leche, por favor.
alsoHeard.where: Also very common and polite across Spain
The same with "usted" — a little more formal

phrases.translation: an espresso with a splash of milk
phrases.example: Para mí, un cortado, por favor.
phrases.note: A "café solo" is a plain espresso; a "café con leche" has much more milk.

phrases.translation: toast with grated tomato (and olive oil)
phrases.example: ¿Me pones una tostada con tomate y aceite?
phrases.exampleTranslation: Can I get toast with tomato and olive oil?
phrases.note: A classic Spanish breakfast: toasted bread topped with grated fresh tomato, olive oil and salt.

phrases.translation: For here or to take away?

phrases.exampleTranslation: Excuse me, can I get another coffee?
phrases.note: "Perdona" (informal) or "perdone" (formal) is a polite way to catch the waiter's attention.

phrases.translation: Can I pay, please? (literally "Can you charge me?")
phrases.exampleTranslation: Excuse me, can I pay when you get a chance?

alsoHeard.where: Understood everywhere, especially at a table

cultureNotes: Breakfast in Spain is usually light — a coffee with toast or a pastry. Many people have a second coffee or a snack mid-morning.
Standing at the bar ("en la barra") is completely normal for a quick breakfast. In some places a table or terrace costs a little more.
You often pay at the end, not when you order — just let the waiter know when you're ready.
Tipping isn't expected in cafés. Rounding up or leaving some small change is a nice gesture if you were happy.

steps.text: You squeeze in at the bar. The waiter wipes the counter in front of you.

steps.speaker: Waiter
steps.translation: Good morning! What can I get you?

steps.prompt: You'd like a coffee with milk. How do you order it?

options.text: ¿Me pones un café con leche, por favor?
options.why: Exactly how locals order in a Spanish bar — natural and friendly.
Understood and grammatically fine, but on its own "quiero" (I want) can sound a little blunt. Adding "por favor", or using "¿me pones…?" or "quería…", softens it.
You'd get a coffee, but with no "un" and no "por favor" it sounds like barking an order — and "café" alone usually means a black espresso, not one with milk.

steps.prompt: You'd like toast topped with grated tomato and olive oil. What do you ask for?

options.text: Una tostada con tomate, por favor.
options.why: That's the classic Spanish breakfast toast.

options.text: Una tortilla con tomate, por favor.
options.why: In Spain a "tortilla" is a thick potato omelette, not bread — and it isn't usually served with tomato. (In Mexico, a tortilla is a flatbread, so the word changes meaning across countries!)
That would be "a toasted tomato". It's the bread ("la tostada") that's toasted, with tomato on top.

steps.speaker: Waiter
steps.translation: For here or to take away?

steps.prompt: What is the waiter asking you?

options.text: Whether you'll have it here or take it away
options.why: "Para tomar aquí" = to have here; "para llevar" = to take away.

options.text: Whether you want it hot or cold
Whether you want to pay now
options.why: Paying comes later. You'd hear something like "Son tres con cincuenta" (That's €3.50) when it's time.

steps.text: You enjoy your breakfast at the bar. A few minutes later you're ready to go, but the waiter is busy at the coffee machine.

steps.prompt: How do you catch his attention and ask to pay?

options.why: Polite and natural: "Excuse me, can I pay when you get a chance?" "La cuenta, por favor" also works anywhere.
It gets the job done, but shouting "Waiter!" sounds rude to most people today. Use "perdona" and "por favor".
This sounds like you want to pay for the table itself. Ask to pay with "¿Me cobras?" or "La cuenta, por favor".

steps.prompt: You pay with a €5 note. What do you do about a tip?

options.text: If you were happy, round up or leave a little change — it's appreciated, not expected.
options.why: Right. Tipping in Spanish cafés is small and optional.

options.text: Leave 15–20%, as in the US — anything less is rude.
options.why: Tipping in Spain is much smaller and optional, especially for a coffee at the bar.

options.text: Never leave anything — tipping is considered insulting.
options.why: It isn't insulting. A little change is a friendly gesture, it just isn't expected.
